chunks: By Allāh, he whom people like you support must suffer disgrace,
and he who throws arrows with your support is as if he throws arrows that are broken both at head and tail.
By Allāh, within the courtyard you are quite numerous but under the Banner you are only a few.
Certainly, I know what can improve you and how your crookedness can be straightened.
But I shall not improve your condition by marring myself.
Allāh may disgrace your faces and destroy you.
You do not understand the right as you understand the wrong and do not crush the wrong as you crush the right.

key_terms.أَفْوَقَ نَاصِلٍ: broken at both ends (head and tail), indicating total uselessness
key_terms.الرَّايَاتِ: banners, symbolizing leadership or true allegiance
key_terms.الْبَاحَاتِ: public courtyards or open places of gathering

ai.seo_question: What does Imam Ali mean by 'broken arrows' in his admonition to his companions?
ai.summary: This passage, often cited in the context of the Battle of Siffin, highlights the tension between the Umayyad faction's numerical superiority in public arenas and their spiritual deficiency. Imam Ali (AS) critiques their 'inverted discernment,' where they recognize falsehood with the same clarity as truth but fail to act upon it, a condition reflecting the historical shift from principled adherence to political expediency. His refusal to compromise his integrity underscores the Shia principle that true leadership requires unwavering fidelity to divine truth, even when outnumbered.
